The same speed throughout; tallest wherever the wind is strongest
Fastest over the deep basin; tallest out in the deep basin as well
Fastest over the deep basin; tallest as it reaches the shallow shelf
rationales: This reverses both. Shallow water slows the wave and makes it taller.
Speed changes with water depth, and wind has no role in a tsunami's height.
In deep water the wave is fast but low. It grows tall only in shallow water.
Correct. Tsunami speed depends on water depth, so it is fastest in deep water. As it enters shallow water it slows and its height increases.
questions.takeaway: Tsunamis are fast and low in deep water, slow and tall in shallow water.

questions.stem: A tsunami spreads out from its source and reaches one coast much later than another coast the same distance away in the opposite direction. What is the best explanation?
options: The slower path ran parallel to the fault, where tsunamis are always weaker
The slower path crossed colder water, which is denser and slows the waves
The water on the slower path is shallower, and tsunami speed depends on depth
The slower path faced a strong headwind, which held the tsunami waves back
rationales: Wave height may vary with direction, but speed is set by depth, not by direction relative to the fault.
Water temperature is not what controls tsunami speed. Depth is.
Correct. Tsunami propagation speed depends on water depth, so the wave travels more slowly across shallower water.
Wind does not control tsunami speed. Water depth does.
questions.takeaway: Tsunami speed depends on water depth, so shallow paths are slower.

questions.stem: Compared with a regular wind-driven wave, why does a tsunami flood so far inland?
options: It is pushed along by strong coastal winds, which drive the water further and further in
It moves only the water near the surface, so all of its energy is packed into the crest
It is much taller out in the deep ocean, so it already towers above ships far offshore
Its wavelength is enormous compared with its height, and it moves the whole water column
rationales: Tsunamis come from sudden displacement of water, not from wind.
This describes a wind-driven wave. A tsunami moves the whole depth of water.
In deep water a tsunami is low; it gains height only as it enters shallow water.
Correct. A tsunami's wavelength is far greater than its height, and unlike a wind wave it moves water all the way down, so a huge volume keeps flowing onshore.
questions.takeaway: Tsunamis have huge wavelengths and move the whole water column, so they surge far inland.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a tsunami-generating mechanism described in the notes?
options: Days of heavy rainfall over a low-lying coastal city
Pyroclastic flows from an eruption entering the sea
An atmospheric pressure wave coupling with the ocean
A submarine landslide down a steep underwater slope
rationales: Correct. Rainfall causes flooding, but it does not suddenly displace a large volume of seawater, so it is not a tsunami mechanism.
Volcanoes can generate tsunamis, including through pyroclastic flows entering the sea.
Meteotsunamis arise from ocean-atmosphere coupling, where a pressure wave drives sea-level change.
Submarine landslides are one of the main tsunami mechanisms.
questions.takeaway: Tsunami mechanisms: earthquakes, volcanoes, submarine landslides and atmospheric pressure waves.

questions.stem: An earthquake on the shallowest part of a subduction interface produces only modest shaking but a very large tsunami. What best explains this?
options: It was a strike-slip event, which makes big tsunamis but little ground shaking
It was a deep event, and deep earthquakes always produce the largest tsunamis
It ruptured slowly, giving weak short-period waves while still moving the seafloor
It ruptured quickly, so most of its energy went into shaking instead of the water
rationales: Strike-slip motion is poor at generating tsunamis. Subduction interfaces rupture as thrusts.
The rupture was shallow, and shallow slip is what lets it move the seafloor so effectively.
Correct. These tsunami earthquakes rupture the shallowest part of the interface slowly, exciting short-period seismic waves weakly compared with their moment and their tsunami.
Fast rupture would produce strong shaking. The modest shaking points to slow rupture.
questions.takeaway: Shallow, slow subduction ruptures can make weak shaking but large tsunamis.

questions.stem: Why can't the size of a tsunami be predicted from an earthquake's magnitude alone?
options: Magnitude comes from intensity reports, which are unreliable for events at sea
Depth, rupture speed and how far the seafloor moves vertically also control it
Tsunamis come from storms that follow earthquakes, not from the earthquakes
Magnitude is not logarithmic, so it understates the size of very large events
rationales: Magnitude is calculated from seismic recordings, not from intensity reports.
Correct. Seismic moment does not correlate perfectly with tsunami size, because rupture depth, speed and vertical seafloor displacement also matter.
Earthquake tsunamis are caused by the seafloor moving during the earthquake itself.
Moment magnitude is logarithmic. The mismatch comes from how the rupture moves the seafloor.
questions.takeaway: Tsunami size depends on how the rupture moves the seafloor, not on magnitude alone.

questions.stem: After an eruption, sea-level disturbances appear at distant coasts, even in ocean basins cut off from the eruption by land. They arrive earlier than any ocean wave could. What most likely caused them?
options: An atmospheric pressure wave coupling with the sea surface along its path
A submarine landslide on the far coast, triggered by the eruption's shaking
A deep ocean current carrying the original wave beneath the land masses
Seismic surface waves that shook the distant coasts and moved the water
rationales: Correct. An atmospheric pressure wave travelling at acoustic speed can couple with the ocean, producing a meteotsunami that crosses land masses and arrives early.
Nothing links simultaneous disturbances in many basins to separate landslides.
Ocean water cannot pass beneath land masses, and currents are far slower than an acoustic pressure wave.
Seismic waves shake the ground, but they would not raise sea level across separate basins in this pattern.
questions.takeaway: Meteotsunami: an atmospheric pressure wave drives sea-level change, even across land.

questions.stem: Which matches each stage of the earthquake cycle to its typical duration?
options: Interseismic: decades to centuries; coseismic: months to years; postseismic: seconds
Interseismic: months to years; coseismic: seconds; postseismic: decades to centuries
Interseismic: decades to centuries; coseismic: seconds; postseismic: months to years
Interseismic: seconds; coseismic: decades to centuries; postseismic: months to years
rationales: Coseismic slip lasts seconds to minutes, and postseismic adjustment lasts much longer than seconds.
Interseismic loading lasts decades or more, and postseismic adjustment lasts days to years, not centuries.
Correct. Strain builds over tens to hundreds of years between earthquakes, is released in seconds to minutes during the rupture, and the crust keeps adjusting for days to years afterwards.
The interseismic stage is the long loading period, not the seconds of rupture.
questions.takeaway: Interseismic (decades–centuries) → coseismic (seconds–minutes) → postseismic (days–years).

questions.stem: A graph of strain on a fault over time shows a long steady rise, a near-vertical drop, then a short curved section before the steady rise resumes. What does the curved section represent?
options: Coseismic slip, as the fault suddenly releases all of its stored stress
A foreshock sequence, as the fault gets ready for its coming mainshock
Interseismic loading, as the locked fault slowly stores up elastic strain
Postseismic adjustment, as afterslip and aftershocks redistribute stress
rationales: Coseismic slip is the near-vertical drop itself.
The curve comes after the earthquake, and foreshocks can only be identified once a larger event follows.
Interseismic loading is the long steady rise, not the short curve after the drop.
Correct. After the sudden coseismic drop, the crust keeps adjusting: stress is redistributed and afterslip and aftershocks may occur over days to years.
questions.takeaway: On a strain–time plot: steady rise = interseismic, sudden drop = coseismic, short curve after = postseismic.

questions.stem: Why does the ground keep deforming for months to years after an earthquake has ended?
options: Seismic waves keep bouncing around in the crust, shaking it for many months
The subsurface is viscoelastic, so it keeps responding to the change in stress
The fault stays unlocked for years and slips steadily at the full plate rate
The plates speed up after an earthquake, so strain builds faster than before
rationales: Seismic waves die away within minutes. They do not cause months of deformation.
Correct. Earth's subsurface is viscoelastic, so it continues to respond to the stress change from the earthquake, producing afterslip and aftershocks.
Afterslip does occur, but the cause is the viscoelastic response to the stress change, not a fault left permanently unlocked.
Plate motion continues at its steady rate; postseismic deformation is the crust adjusting to the stress change.
questions.takeaway: Postseismic deformation reflects the viscoelastic response of the subsurface to the earthquake's stress change.

questions.stem: Two faults are loaded by plate motion at the same rate. Fault X releases strain in frequent small earthquakes, while fault Y stays locked for a much longer interseismic period. Compared with X's events, Y's next earthquake is likely to be:
options: Smaller, since a long locked period lets the strain leak away quietly
The same size, since both faults are loaded at exactly the same rate
Impossible to compare, since interseismic strain cannot be measured
Larger, since more strain has built up over its longer locked period
rationales: A locked fault stores strain rather than losing it. That is the basis of elastic rebound.
Loading rate is the same, but the size of an earthquake depends on how much strain has accumulated before it slips.
Interseismic strain can be measured, for example with GNSS stations recording slow motion over years.
Correct. On the strain–time plot, the longer the strain accumulates, the larger the drop when the fault finally slips.
questions.takeaway: A longer locked period stores more strain, which tends to mean a larger earthquake.

questions.stem: Why are GNSS stations used for plate motion securely anchored to bedrock?
options: So they record motion of the crust itself, precise to under a millimetre a year
So the solid rock shields them from radio interference that blocks satellite signals
So they can sense heat rising from the mantle beneath the moving plates
So they can measure shaking intensity directly from the rock beneath them
rationales: Correct. Anchoring to bedrock means the receiver moves with the crust, and these high-precision receivers can track movement of less than a millimetre per year.
Bedrock anchoring is about moving with the crust, not about blocking interference.
GNSS tracks position; it does not measure heat.
GNSS measures position over time, not shaking intensity.
questions.takeaway: GNSS stations on bedrock track crustal motion precisely enough to monitor plate motion.

questions.stem: Why is radar better suited than optical imagery for mapping ground changes after an earthquake in a cloudy tropical region?
options: It measures shaking intensity from the colour of the ground
It sees only at night, when the ground echoes are clearest
It works by day and night and can see through clouds
It uses visible light, so it takes sharper images than optical
rationales: Radar measures echoes from the ground, not the colour of the ground or shaking intensity.
Radar works day and night; it is not limited to night.
Correct. Radar has all-day capability and nearly all-weather capability, so it can see through clouds that block optical images.
Radar uses microwaves, not visible light. That is why it can see through cloud.
questions.takeaway: Radar sees through cloud, day or night, which optical imagery cannot.

questions.stem: InSAR compares the phase of radar echoes from two passes over the same ground. What does a phase shift between the passes represent?
options: A change in surface temperature between the passes, caused by friction on the fault
Ground displacement along the satellite's line of sight between the two passes
Ground displacement in the north–south direction only, whatever the satellite path
A difference in cloud cover between the two passes, which must then be removed
rationales: The phase shift reflects ground movement, not temperature.
Correct. Phase shift equals displacement along the line of sight, so comparing passes before and after movement maps how the ground moved.
InSAR measures motion along the satellite's line of sight, not one fixed compass direction.
Radar sees through cloud, so cloud cover is not what the phase shift records.
questions.takeaway: InSAR phase shift = ground displacement along the satellite's line of sight.

questions.stem: Before an interferogram can be used to measure fault slip, which effects must be corrected for?
options: Ocean tides, shaking intensity and the depth of the hypocentre
Cloud cover, time of day and the season the images were taken
Topography, satellite positions and the curvature of the Earth
Building heights, road layouts and the population living there
rationales: These are not part of turning phase differences into ground displacement.
Radar sees through cloud and works day and night, so these are not the corrections listed.
Correct. An interferogram (phase A minus phase B) must be corrected for topography, satellite positions and Earth's curvature.
These describe exposure, not corrections to the radar phase.
questions.takeaway: Interferograms are corrected for topography, satellite positions and Earth's curvature.

questions.stem: A team wants to track the slow build-up of strain across a plate boundary over a decade. Which tool fits best?
options: A network of GNSS stations recording position continuously for years
A DART buoy measuring changes in water pressure on the seafloor
A shaking intensity survey compiled from damage after each event
A single seismometer that records the shaking during the next large earthquake
rationales: Correct. Interseismic strain builds slowly, and GNSS stations can track sub-millimetre motion per year, which suits monitoring this stage.
DART buoys detect tsunamis in the ocean, not strain across a plate boundary.
Intensity surveys record damage from one earthquake, not slow strain build-up.
A seismometer records the sudden coseismic stage, not slow loading between earthquakes.
questions.takeaway: GNSS is the tool for slow interseismic strain; seismometers capture coseismic rupture.

questions.stem: Which observation best reveals how fast a fault slips during the rupture itself?
options: Building damage surveys completed weeks after the earthquake
GNSS positions averaged over the decade before the earthquake
Tsunami deposits found in coastal sediments after the event
Seismometer records of ground motion during the earthquake
rationales: Damage surveys measure intensity, not the slip on the fault.
Averages over the decade before capture interseismic loading, not the rupture.
Deposits show that a past tsunami happened, not how fast a fault slipped.
Correct. Seismometers record the coseismic stage directly and can show how fast the fault slips over the seconds of rupture.
questions.takeaway: Seismometers capture the coseismic stage as it happens.

questions.stem: A large earthquake strikes a remote area with no ground-based instruments. How can scientists still map where the fault ruptured and how much it slipped?
options: Install GNSS stations right after the event to record its coseismic slip
Compare radar images from before and after to map surface displacement
Use optical images taken at night to detect heat released along the fault
Wait for the aftershocks to stop, then add up their total released energy
rationales: Stations installed after the event miss the coseismic slip they would be trying to record.
Correct. InSAR compares radar passes from before and after the earthquake to detect surface change and show how much the fault slipped.
Optical images need daylight and clear skies, and they do not measure heat from slip.
Aftershock energy does not map the rupture or its slip.
questions.takeaway: InSAR maps coseismic displacement from space, even where there are no ground instruments.

questions.stem: Why can an earthquake not be identified as a foreshock at the moment it happens?
options: It only counts as a foreshock once a larger earthquake follows nearby
Foreshocks happen deep in the mantle, beyond the reach of monitoring
Foreshocks are too small to be located until the aftershocks begin
Foreshocks produce no S waves, so seismometers record them as noise
rationales: Correct. Foreshocks are earthquakes that precede larger ones in the same place, so one can only be called a foreshock after the larger earthquake occurs.
Foreshocks occur in the same location as the following larger earthquake, not deep in the mantle.
Size is not the issue. The label depends on whether a larger event follows.
Foreshocks are ordinary earthquakes with ordinary seismic waves.
questions.takeaway: A foreshock is defined only in hindsight, after a larger earthquake follows.

questions.stem: Ten days after a large mainshock, a resident says the remaining aftershocks must now be too small to cause harm. Which response fits the notes?
options: Aftershocks become more frequent over time, but each one is much smaller
That's right, because no aftershock can occur more than a week after the event
That's right, because aftershocks get steadily smaller with every passing day
Aftershocks become less frequent with time, but their magnitudes do not shrink
rationales: The rate of aftershocks falls with time rather than rising.
Aftershocks can continue for days to years after the mainshock.
This is the misconception the notes warn against: magnitudes do not decline over time.
Correct. The rate of aftershocks decreases with time, but their magnitudes do not get smaller. Only their rate changes.
questions.takeaway: Aftershock rate falls with time; aftershock size does not.

questions.stem: Two mainshocks of very different sizes strike similar regions. Which expectation is supported by the statistics in the notes?
options: Neither triggers aftershocks unless a foreshock came first
The larger mainshock is likely to trigger more aftershocks
The smaller mainshock is likely to trigger more aftershocks
Both trigger the same number, since aftershocks are random
rationales: Aftershocks follow mainshocks whether or not there was a foreshock.
Correct. Larger mainshocks trigger more aftershocks than smaller mainshocks.
This reverses the relationship.
Aftershock occurrence can be estimated statistically, and it scales with the size of the mainshock.
questions.takeaway: Bigger mainshocks trigger more aftershocks.

questions.stem: Compared with the first day after a mainshock, roughly how many aftershocks would you expect on the tenth day?
options: About half as many
About ten times as many
About a tenth as many
About the same number
rationales: The decline is steeper than this. The notes give about a tenth as many by the tenth day.
The rate decreases with time, not increases.
Correct. The aftershock rate decreases with time: there are about ten times as many aftershocks on the first day as on the tenth.
The rate falls with time, so the numbers are not the same.
questions.takeaway: Aftershock rate decays with time: about ten times fewer on day ten than on day one.

questions.stem: A moderate earthquake has just occurred. What do the statistics in the notes suggest about a larger earthquake nearby within the following week?
options: A small but real chance, so it cannot be ruled out
It is impossible, since the stress is now released
It is likely, as most quakes are followed by bigger ones
It is certain, since every quake leads to a bigger one
rationales: Correct. The chance of an earthquake being followed by a larger one nearby within a week is about 5%: small, but real.
The stress change can bring other parts of the fault closer to failure, so a larger event is possible.
The chance is small, about 5%, so a larger one is not likely.
Most earthquakes are not followed by a larger one, so it is not certain.
questions.takeaway: There is a small but real chance (about 5%) that an earthquake is followed by a larger one within a week.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes aftershocks?
options: Echoes of the mainshock's seismic waves, recorded again as they bounce back
Larger earthquakes that follow a mainshock once its fault has fully unlocked
Earthquakes that occur only on faults far away from the one that slipped
Smaller earthquakes nearby as the crust readjusts after a larger mainshock
rationales: Aftershocks are real earthquakes, not echoes of earlier waves.
A larger earthquake would itself become the mainshock, turning the first event into a foreshock.
Aftershocks occur in the same general area, mostly along the part of the fault that slipped.
Correct. Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes in the same general area during the days to years after a mainshock, representing readjustments along the fault that slipped.
questions.takeaway: Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes in the same area as the crust readjusts after a mainshock.

questions.stem: Above a locked subduction zone, a coastal bulge rises slowly over decades while an area further landward sinks. What happens when the megathrust finally slips in an earthquake?
options: Nothing changes vertically, as these earthquakes move land sideways only
The motions reverse: the bulge drops and the landward area rises
Both areas rise together, as the rupture lifts the whole margin upward
The motions continue: the bulge rises faster and the land sinks more
rationales: Megathrust earthquakes cause large vertical changes, both uplift and subsidence.
Correct. As strain accumulates, a bulge rises and a landward area sinks. These vertical displacements reverse when the fault slips.
The rupture produces a pattern of both uplift and subsidence, not uniform uplift.
The earthquake releases the strain that caused these motions, so they reverse rather than speed up.
questions.takeaway: At subduction zones, vertical motions built up between earthquakes reverse when the megathrust slips.

questions.stem: After a megathrust earthquake, a harbour dock is left so high above the water that boats can no longer use it. What does this indicate?
options: Sea level fell sharply because the tsunami drained the water out of the bay
The coast subsided during rupture, which drew the sea away from the dock
The coast was uplifted as the overriding plate rebounded during the rupture
Postseismic afterslip slowly lifted the seabed over the following decade
rationales: A tsunami's water returns; it does not permanently lower sea level.
Subsidence would lower the land, bringing the sea closer to the dock, not further away.
Correct. Megathrust slip produces uplift in some areas, raising the coast and leaving docks stranded above the water.
The change was abrupt, linked to the earthquake itself, not a slow decade-long process.
questions.takeaway: Megathrust earthquakes can abruptly uplift coasts, stranding docks above the sea.

questions.stem: A GPS station on an island near a trench moves steadily landward for years, then jumps back seaward during a large earthquake. What does this illustrate?
options: Elastic rebound: strain stored during loading is released in the rupture
Postseismic afterslip: the fault creeps backward before locking up again
Mantle convection: the plate turns around once the slab breaks away below
Induced seismicity: fluid pressure pushes the island back during the slip
rationales: Correct. The motion before the earthquake is relieved during it, an example of Reid's elastic rebound theory.
The jump happened during the earthquake, so it is coseismic rather than postseismic.
The plates do not reverse direction. The station's jump is the release of stored elastic strain.
Induced seismicity involves human activity raising fluid pressure, which plays no part here.
questions.takeaway: GPS motion that is reversed during an earthquake is elastic rebound in action.

questions.stem: During a megathrust earthquake, where does uplift typically occur relative to subsidence?
options: Subsidence nearer the trench, with uplift further landward
Uplift everywhere, with the most uplift furthest inland
Subsidence everywhere, with the most along the coastline
Uplift nearer the trench, with subsidence further landward
rationales: This reverses the pattern shown in the notes.
The rupture produces both uplift and subsidence, not uplift everywhere.
The rupture produces both uplift and subsidence, not subsidence everywhere.
Correct. Slip on the megathrust uplifts the area nearer the trench and lowers the area further landward. Where the coast sits relative to the trench decides what happens there.
questions.takeaway: Megathrust slip: uplift towards the trench, subsidence further landward.

questions.stem: Why does an earthquake early warning system give little or no warning to places right next to the epicentre?
options: Warning messages travel more slowly than seismic waves, so they arrive late
Shaking near the epicentre comes only from P waves, which give no warning
The damaging S and surface waves arrive almost as soon as the first P waves
P waves cannot be detected near the epicentre, because they are too large
rationales: Warning messages travel at the speed of light, much faster than seismic waves.
Near the epicentre the damaging S and surface waves still arrive. They just follow the P waves too closely.
Correct. Warnings rely on fast P waves arriving before the damaging S and surface waves. Close to the source the gap between them is tiny, leaving a blind zone.
P waves near the source are readily detected; the problem is how little time separates them from the S waves.
questions.takeaway: Early warning uses the gap between P waves and damaging S waves, and that gap is tiny near the source.

questions.stem: What does a DART station detect, and how?
options: Earthquakes, using a seafloor seismometer linked to a coastal radar
Tsunamis, using a seafloor pressure recorder linked to a surface buoy
Storm surges, using a buoy that measures how wind speed is changing
Tsunamis, using a surface buoy that films the wave height from above
rationales: DART is designed for tsunamis, using water pressure, not seismometers and radar.
Correct. Each DART station has a surface buoy and a seafloor bottom pressure recorder, which detects water pressure changes caused by tsunamis.
DART detects tsunamis through water pressure changes, not storm surges through wind.
Detection relies on the seafloor pressure recorder, not filming the waves.
questions.takeaway: DART: seafloor pressure recorder plus surface buoy, detecting tsunamis in the deep ocean.

questions.stem: Tsunami warning systems can give an hour to a day of warning. Which community benefits most from deep-ocean tsunami detection?
options: A coast right next to the source, reached minutes after the earthquake
A coast across the ocean basin, many hours' travel from the source
A coast where the earthquake struck under land, far from any sea
A coast inland of a mountain range, where the tsunami cannot reach
rationales: Near-source coasts may be hit before detection, assessment and warning can happen.
Correct. Distant coasts have hours before arrival, which gives time for buoys to detect the tsunami and warnings to be issued.
An earthquake under land does not displace seawater, so there is no tsunami to detect.
A coast the tsunami cannot reach has no need of warning.
questions.takeaway: Deep-ocean tsunami warnings help most where travel times are long.

questions.stem: A densely populated coastal city sits on flat land near a subduction zone, with little high ground within reach. Which measure from the notes best addresses this?
options: Vertical evacuation structures that people can climb to escape the tsunami
A DART buoy placed just offshore to warn the city well before the wave
Placing coastal pipelines on sliders so the ground can move beneath them
Restricting land use within a fixed distance of every active fault trace
rationales: Correct. Where people cannot reach high ground in time, vertical evacuation structures provide height. One proposal doubles as a community park in normal times.
Near a subduction zone the tsunami may arrive within minutes, so a nearby buoy does not buy enough time.
Pipeline sliders protect against fault offset, not tsunami flooding.
Fault zoning addresses surface rupture, not tsunami flooding.
questions.takeaway: Vertical evacuation structures give height where natural high ground is out of reach.

questions.stem: Laws that restrict building within a set distance of active fault traces mainly target which hazard?
options: Aftershocks that keep occurring for years after a mainshock
Tsunami flooding of low-lying ground close to the coastline
Surface rupture tearing through structures built across the fault
Strong shaking amplified by soft sediments in nearby sedimentary basins
rationales: Aftershocks shake a wide area; a setback from the fault trace does not address them.
Tsunami flooding is managed with hazard maps, warnings and evacuation, not fault setbacks.
Correct. Fault zone laws restrict land use on active faults because buildings sitting on the rupture are torn apart, while similar buildings nearby can survive.
Basin amplification affects whole regions, not a narrow strip along the fault.
questions.takeaway: Fault zoning targets surface rupture, which destroys buildings built on the fault.

questions.stem: A pipeline must cross an active strike-slip fault. Which design approach does the notes highlight?
options: Bury the pipe deep so the fault offset passes harmlessly above the pipeline
Anchor the pipe rigidly on both sides so that it holds the two blocks together
Run the pipe along the fault trace so it shifts together with the slip
Rest the pipe on sliders so the ground can shift beneath it without breaking it
rationales: Fault offset extends to depth, so burying the pipe would put it right in the path of the slip.
A pipe cannot hold back plate motion; rigid anchoring would make it snap.
The two sides of a strike-slip fault move in opposite directions, so a pipe along the trace would still be torn.
Correct. A pipeline placed on sliders let the ground move beneath it during fault offset without breaking it.
questions.takeaway: Designing for fault offset (e.g. sliders) lets infrastructure survive surface rupture.

questions.stem: Instrumental records near a subduction zone cover only about a century. How can scientists judge whether very large tsunamis have struck there before?
options: Study tsunami deposits, drowned forests and corals that record past events
Extrapolate from present GNSS motion, which records every past earthquake
Use InSAR images, which reveal displacements from previous centuries
Count today's aftershocks, as their number reveals the largest past event
rationales: Correct. Tsunami deposits, ghost forests drowned by subsidence, and corals that track past uplift extend the record far beyond instruments.
GNSS measures present motion only; it does not record earthquakes before the stations existed.
InSAR satellites have only operated recently, so they cannot see centuries back.
Present aftershock counts relate to recent mainshocks, not the region's largest past event.
questions.takeaway: Geological records such as deposits, drowned forests and corals reveal past tsunamis and earthquakes.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of tsunami hazard maps and warning signs?
options: Predict the exact date and size of the next tsunami along a given coastline
Prevent tsunamis by marking where seafloor slip is most likely to happen
Record the heights of past tsunamis for settling insurance claims later
Support emergency planning and adaptation by showing where water may reach
rationales: Hazard maps show where flooding could reach; they do not predict exact timing.
Maps cannot prevent tsunamis. They help people prepare for them.
Their purpose is preparedness, not recording past events for insurance.
Correct. Hazard maps and warning signs help communities with infrastructural adaptation and emergency planning.
questions.takeaway: Tsunami hazard maps and signs support planning and evacuation.

questions.stem: After a thrust earthquake, buildings standing across the fault trace collapsed while similar buildings a short distance away survived. What does this show?
options: Shaking was weaker on the fault trace than further away from the fault
Rupture beneath a structure does far more damage than shaking alone
Only buildings over the hypocentre collapse, as shaking is focused there
Buildings away from the trace were saved by soft ground absorbing waves
rationales: Shaking is generally strongest close to the source, so it would not be weaker on the trace.
Correct. Buildings not on the fault did not collapse, while buildings on it were torn apart by the surface rupture.
The rupture runs along the fault trace at the surface; the hypocentre is a single point at depth.
Soft ground amplifies shaking rather than absorbing it.
questions.takeaway: Surface rupture destroys buildings on the fault, which is why fault zoning matters.

questions.stem: Why do the notes stress cooperation between countries in managing tsunami risk?
options: Each country's warning system only works for tsunamis inside its own borders
Tsunamis form only in international waters that no single country controls
A tsunami from one country's subduction zone can strike coasts in many others
Tsunami building codes must be identical in every country before they work
rationales: Warning systems share data across borders. The point is that the hazard itself crosses borders.
Tsunamis can start close to any country's coast, not only in international waters.
Correct. Natural hazards are transboundary: tsunamis cross ocean basins, so detection and warnings need countries to cooperate.
Nothing requires identical codes. Cooperation matters because the hazard crosses borders.
questions.takeaway: Hazards like tsunamis are transboundary, so countries must cooperate.

questions.stem: Mantle rock at a fixed depth begins to melt even though its temperature has not risen. Which change could explain this?
options: Extra rock piled up above it, raising the pressure that acts on it at that depth
Slower plate motion overhead, letting the rock cool down and then contract
Water driven out of the rock, raising the temperature needed for melting
Water added from a subducting slab, lowering the temperature needed to melt
rationales: Increasing pressure makes rock harder to melt, not easier. Melting comes from decreasing pressure.
Cooling works against melting, and plate speed overhead does not melt the rock.
Removing water would raise the melting temperature, making melting less likely.
Correct. Adding water reduces the temperature needed to melt rock (flux melting), so rock can melt without heating up or moving.
questions.takeaway: Magma forms by adding heat, lowering pressure, or adding water; at fixed depth and temperature, only water can do it.

questions.stem: At a mid-ocean ridge, mantle rock rises and melts. What triggers the melting?
options: Friction between the separating plates heats the rock beyond its melting point
Water from a sinking slab lowers the melting point of the rising mantle rock
Pressure falls as the rock rises, while its temperature stays about the same
Temperature rises sharply as the rock rises, while the pressure stays the same
rationales: Friction between plates does not melt the mantle at ridges.
Water-driven (flux) melting happens at subduction zones, where slabs carry water down. There is no sinking slab at a ridge.
Correct. This is decompression melting: as rock rises from mantle to crust its temperature stays about the same while pressure drops, so it melts.
The rising rock does not heat up sharply. The change that matters is falling pressure.
questions.takeaway: Mid-ocean ridges: decompression melting as rising rock loses pressure.

questions.stem: Which pairing of tectonic setting with its main melting process is correct?
options: Mid-ocean ridge: decompression melting; subduction zone: water lowering the melting point
Mid-ocean ridge: friction between plates; subduction zone: pressure rise melting the slab
Mid-ocean ridge: rising pressure on the rock; subduction zone: friction between the plates
Mid-ocean ridge: water lowering the melting point; subduction zone: decompression melting
rationales: Correct. Rock rising beneath ridges melts as pressure drops; at subduction zones, water released from the slab lowers the melting temperature of the mantle above.
Neither friction nor rising pressure melts rock in these settings; rising pressure actually hinders melting.
Rising pressure hinders melting, and friction is not the melting process at subduction zones.
The two processes are swapped.
questions.takeaway: Ridges melt by decompression; subduction zones melt by adding water (flux melting).

questions.stem: In a continental rift, the cold upper part of the plate breaks along normal faults, and volcanoes appear along the fault boundaries. Where does their magma come from?
options: Friction on the normal faults heating the crust until it partly melts
Hot, ductile upper mantle rising beneath the thinning plate and melting
A subducting slab beneath the rift releasing water into the mantle above
Old ocean lithosphere pushed onto the continent and melted by collision
rationales: The normal faults break the brittle upper plate, but the magma comes from rising mantle, not fault friction.
Correct. As divergence pulls the continent apart, hot, ductile upper mantle rises, elevating the land and generating magma that feeds volcanism along the faults.
Rifts are divergent settings; there is no subducting slab supplying water beneath them.
Ocean lithosphere placed on a continent by collision is an ophiolite. It does not feed rift volcanism.
questions.takeaway: Continental rift volcanism: rising, decompressing upper mantle beneath a stretching plate.

questions.stem: A curved chain of volcanic islands forms where one oceanic plate sinks beneath another oceanic plate. Which setting is this?
options: An ocean-ocean convergent boundary, forming a volcanic island arc
A divergent boundary, where islands form along the spreading ridge
A hotspot track, where islands form as a plate moves over a plume
An ocean-continent convergent boundary, forming a continental arc
rationales: Correct. Chains of volcanic islands form where oceanic plates subduct beneath other oceanic plates, at an ocean-ocean convergent boundary.
Spreading ridges produce new ocean floor, not an arc of islands above a sinking plate.
Hotspot chains form within a plate, not where one plate sinks beneath another.
A continental arc needs an ocean plate subducting under a continent, but here both plates are oceanic.
questions.takeaway: Ocean-ocean subduction builds volcanic island arcs; ocean-continent subduction builds continental arcs.

questions.stem: A line of stratovolcanoes runs parallel to a coastline, inland of a deep ocean trench. What best explains their location?
options: A transform boundary runs along the coast, where sliding heats the rock up to its melting point
A stationary hotspot lies under the coast and feeds each of the volcanoes in turn
The continent is rifting apart, so decompression melting happens along the coast
An oceanic plate subducts beneath the continent, adding water that melts the mantle
rationales: Transform boundaries do not generate magma by sliding.
A hotspot under a moving plate makes a chain that ages along its length, not an arc running beside a trench.
A trench points to convergence, not rifting.
Correct. The trench marks subduction; water released from the sinking slab causes melting in the mantle above, building a continental volcanic arc inland.
questions.takeaway: Trench plus parallel line of volcanoes = subduction-related volcanic arc.

questions.stem: What is the source of a hotspot?
options: A subducting slab releasing water into the mantle beneath the moving plate
A mantle plume rising from deep in the mantle, near the core-mantle boundary
A divergent boundary where two plates pull apart and thin the crust above
Friction on a transform fault that heats rock along the length of the plate
rationales: Slab water drives arc volcanism at subduction zones, not hotspots.
Correct. Hotspots are fed by a mantle plume rising from the core-mantle boundary.
Hotspots occur within plates, away from divergent boundaries.
Transform faults do not produce hotspot magma.
questions.takeaway: Hotspots are fed by mantle plumes rising from the core-mantle boundary.

questions.stem: A plate moves over a stationary hotspot, building a chain of volcanoes. Partway through, the plate changes the direction it is moving. What would the chain show?
options: Two parallel chains, because the plume splits to follow both directions
No change, because the hotspot moves with the plate and keeps a straight line
A bend, because the chain records the plate's path over a fixed source
A gap, because hotspots switch off whenever the plate's motion changes
rationales: A single plume makes a single track; it does not split.
The hotspot stays roughly stationary; it is the plate that moves.
Correct. Because the hotspot is stationary, the chain traces the plate's motion over it. A change in direction shows up as a bend in the track.
The plume keeps supplying magma regardless of plate direction.
questions.takeaway: A hotspot track records the plate's motion over a fixed plume, so a turn in motion bends the chain.

questions.stem: On a hotspot island chain, the only active volcano is at the eastern end, and the islands become older towards the west. Which way is the plate moving?
options: Westward, carrying older volcanoes away from the hotspot
It is not moving, while the hotspot drifts to the east
Westward, but only because the hotspot moves west too
Eastward, carrying older volcanoes towards the hotspot
rationales: Correct. The active volcano sits over the stationary hotspot. As the plate moves west, it carries each volcano away from the magma source, so they get older westward.
Hotspots are treated as stationary; the plate does the moving.
The plate's motion alone explains the pattern; the hotspot stays put.
If the plate moved east, older islands would lie to the east of the active one.
questions.takeaway: In a hotspot chain, volcanoes get older in the direction the plate is moving.

questions.stem: Hotspot volcanoes can form beneath both oceans and continents. What sets a hotspot volcano apart from an arc volcano?
options: It forms where plates diverge, while arcs form where plates slide past
It forms only beneath oceans, while arcs form only beneath the continents
It forms within a plate above a plume, not from slab water at a boundary
It forms by water lowering melting points, while arcs form by decompression
rationales: Hotspots are not divergent boundaries, and arcs form at convergent boundaries, not where plates slide past.
Continental hotspots exist, and arcs can be oceanic island arcs.
Correct. Hotspots sit over a mantle plume, often far from plate boundaries, while arc volcanoes form above subducting slabs that release water.
This swaps the mechanisms: water-driven melting is what feeds arcs.
questions.takeaway: Hotspot volcanoes sit over plumes within plates; arc volcanoes sit over subducting slabs.

questions.stem: Why does rock in a rising mantle plume melt as it nears the base of the plate?
options: The pressure on it increases as it rises toward the surface
It stays very hot while the pressure on it falls as it rises
Water from a nearby subducting slab lowers its melting point
Friction with the moving plate above heats it until it melts
rationales: Pressure decreases, not increases, as rock rises.
Correct. High heat combined with lower pressure helps the plume rock melt. The melt then rises through cracks to form volcanoes.
Hotspots are not tied to subducting slabs.
Friction with the plate is not the cause of hotspot melting.
questions.takeaway: Plume rock melts because it stays hot while the pressure on it drops.

questions.stem: Which pairing of magma type with its silica content and viscosity is correct?
options: Felsic: high silica, low viscosity; mafic: low silica, high viscosity
Felsic: low silica, high viscosity; mafic: high silica, low viscosity
Felsic: low silica, low viscosity; mafic: high silica, high viscosity
Felsic: high silica, high viscosity; mafic: low silica, low viscosity
rationales: More silica makes magma stiffer, so high silica goes with high viscosity.
Low silica gives low viscosity, not high.
This is the version on the original Week 5 slide, which was corrected in Week 6.
Correct. Felsic is full of silica and more viscous; mafic is missing silica and less viscous. Week 6 opened by correcting this pairing on the Week 5 slide.
questions.takeaway: Felsic = full of silica = more viscous; mafic = missing silica = less viscous.

questions.stem: An igneous rock has large, clearly visible crystals. What does this indicate about how it formed?
options: It cooled slowly inside the Earth, so it is intrusive
It cooled quickly at the surface, so it is extrusive
It cooled slowly at the surface, so it is extrusive
It cooled quickly inside the Earth, so it is intrusive
rationales: Correct. Intrusive rocks cool slowly inside the Earth, giving crystals time to grow large (coarse grained).
Quick cooling at the surface gives fine grains, not large crystals.
Rock at the surface cools quickly, so extrusive rocks are fine grained.
Rock inside the Earth stays hot and cools slowly, which is why intrusive crystals are large.
questions.takeaway: Intrusive = inside, slow cooling, big crystals; extrusive = exits, fast cooling, fine grains.

questions.stem: Large amounts of pumice are produced in Plinian eruptions. How should pumice be classified?
options: Mafic and intrusive
Felsic and extrusive
Felsic and intrusive
Mafic and extrusive
rationales: Pumice is neither mafic nor formed underground.
Correct. Pumice comes from high-silica magma blasted out at the surface, so it is felsic and extrusive.
Pumice forms from magma erupted at the surface, so it is extrusive.
Plinian eruptions involve high-silica rhyolitic magma, which is felsic, not mafic.
questions.takeaway: Pumice: felsic, extrusive, typical of Plinian eruptions.

questions.stem: Magma A has a low silica content; magma B has a much higher silica content. As each rises and its gases form bubbles, which is more likely to erupt explosively?
options: Magma A, because low-silica magma can hold more gas under pressure
Neither, because silica controls volcano shape but not eruption style
Magma A, because its fluidity lets bubbles grow much larger before escaping
Magma B, because its stiffness traps gas bubbles until pressure builds
rationales: The notes link explosivity to gas being trapped by stiff, high-silica magma, not to low-silica magma.
Magma type controls both the shape of the volcano and its eruption style.
In fluid magma bubbles escape easily, which is why low-silica eruptions are effusive.
Correct. More silica makes magma stiffer. Bubbles cannot escape easily from viscous magma, so pressure builds until the gas violently fragments it.
questions.takeaway: High silica, stiff magma traps gas, which leads to explosive eruptions.

questions.stem: Basalt and rhyolite are both extrusive rocks. What separates them?
options: Basalt is intrusive, while rhyolite forms only at hotspot volcanoes
Basalt is felsic and formed from stiff lava; rhyolite is mafic and fluid
Basalt is mafic and formed from fluid lava; rhyolite is felsic and stiff
Basalt cooled slowly underground, while rhyolite cooled at the surface
rationales: Basalt is extrusive, and rhyolite is not limited to hotspots.
The magma types are swapped.
Correct. Basalt has roughly half silica and is fluid; rhyolite has much more silica and is stiff. Both are extrusive.
Both are extrusive, so both cooled at the surface.
questions.takeaway: Basalt: mafic, fluid. Rhyolite: felsic, stiff.

questions.stem: Which combination makes lava flow most easily?
options: Hotter lava with high silica content
Hotter lava with low silica content
Cooler lava with high silica content
Cooler lava with low silica content
rationales: High silica makes lava stiff, even when hot.
Correct. Shield volcano lavas are hotter, low in silica and less viscous, so they flow most easily.
Both factors point to stiff lava.
Low silica helps, but cooler lava is stiffer than hotter lava.
questions.takeaway: Hot, low-silica lava is the most fluid.

questions.stem: Why do shield volcanoes have broad shapes and gentle slopes?
options: Their explosive eruptions scatter material across wide areas
Their stiff, high-silica lava piles up close around the vent
Their fluid, low-silica lava flows far before it solidifies
Their magma cools underground, lifting the land up gently
rationales: Shield volcano eruptions are mostly non-explosive.
Stiff lava piling up near the vent builds steeper stratovolcanoes.
Correct. The fluidity of shield volcano lava gives a low aspect ratio: lava spreads widely, building broad, gentle slopes.
Shield volcanoes are built from erupted lava, not uplift from cooling magma.
questions.takeaway: Fluid lava spreads widely and builds broad, gentle shield volcanoes.

questions.stem: Which comparison of shield volcanoes and stratovolcanoes is correct?
options: Shield: smaller, built of stiff lava; strato: larger, built of fluid basaltic lava
Shield: steep-sided and rhyolitic; strato: gentle slopes and built from basalt
Shield: high aspect ratio, mostly explosive; strato: low aspect ratio, mostly effusive
Shield: low aspect ratio, mostly effusive; strato: steeper, can be explosive
rationales: Shield volcanoes are far larger than stratovolcanoes, and they are built of fluid lava.
Shields are gentle and basaltic; stratovolcanoes are steeper and closer to rhyolitic.
The descriptions are swapped.
Correct. Fluid lava gives shields a low aspect ratio and mostly non-explosive eruptions. Viscous lava gives stratovolcanoes a higher aspect ratio, with explosive and non-explosive eruptions.
questions.takeaway: Shield: broad, fluid, effusive. Strato: steep, viscous, can be explosive.

questions.stem: A student assumes the tallest, steepest-looking volcanoes must also be the largest. What do the notes show?
options: Shield volcanoes are far larger overall, despite their gentle slopes
Stratovolcanoes are largest, because steep sides hold more volume
Cinder cones are largest, because they grow through many eruptions
All volcano types reach similar sizes; only their slopes differ
rationales: Correct. Shield volcanoes are far larger than stratovolcanoes; much of a shield's bulk can even sit below sea level.
Steepness reflects viscous lava, not size. Stratovolcanoes are much smaller than shields.
Cinder cones are even smaller than stratovolcanoes.
Sizes differ enormously between volcano types.
questions.takeaway: Gentle shield volcanoes are by far the largest volcano type.

questions.stem: Why do gases drive explosions in viscous magma but escape quietly from fluid magma?
options: In viscous magma, expanding bubbles cannot escape, so pressure builds
Viscous magma rises faster, so its gas stays dissolved the whole way
Fluid magma traps its bubbles more tightly, so the gas cannot expand
Viscous magma holds no dissolved gas, so pressure comes from heat alone
rationales: Correct. In thick, viscous magma the bubbles cannot escape easily, so pressure keeps building until expanding gases violently fragment the magma.
Gases come out of solution as pressure falls on the way up, whatever the magma type.
This reverses it: in fluid magma, bubbles expand and escape easily.
Viscous magma does hold dissolved gas; that gas is what drives the explosion.
questions.takeaway: Viscous magma traps expanding gas like a pressure cooker; fluid magma lets it escape.

questions.stem: As magma rises towards the surface, what role does the falling pressure around it play?
options: It cools the magma until it solidifies in the vent
It raises the silica content of the rising magma
It forces gases to dissolve more fully in the magma
It lets dissolved gases form bubbles and expand
rationales: The key effect of falling pressure is on the gas, not on cooling the magma.
Pressure does not change the magma's silica content.
Falling pressure does the opposite: it lets gas come out of solution.
Correct. Deep down, high pressure keeps gases dissolved. As pressure decreases during ascent, gases form bubbles and expand.
questions.takeaway: Falling pressure on rising magma lets dissolved gases bubble out and expand.

questions.stem: Which lists the regions of a Plinian eruption column in order, from the vent upward?
options: Convective, then gas thrust, then umbrella
Gas thrust, then convective, then umbrella
Umbrella, then convective, then gas thrust
Gas thrust, then umbrella, then convective
rationales: The gas thrust region is the lowest part, where material is blasted out of the vent.
Correct. The lowest kilometre or two is the gas thrust region, then the convective region, then the umbrella region at the top.
This is the order from the top down.
The umbrella region is the uppermost part, above the convective region.
questions.takeaway: Plinian column, bottom to top: gas thrust → convective → umbrella.

questions.stem: In the lowest region of a Plinian eruption column, what mainly drives material upward?
options: Buoyancy of the hot gas and ash mixture rising by convection
Sideways spreading of the column once it reaches its top height
The force of expanding gas blasting material out of the vent
Wind shear lifting fine ash vertically away from the crater
rationales: Buoyant convection takes over in the next region up, the convective region.
Sideways spreading happens in the umbrella region at the top.
Correct. The lowest part is the gas thrust region, where the blast of expanding gas propels material upward.
Wind does not push the column vertically.
questions.takeaway: Gas thrust drives the lowest part of a Plinian column; convection drives the middle.

questions.stem: A photo shows ash spreading sideways into a broad, flat cloud high above an erupting volcano. Which part of the Plinian column is this?
options: The convective region, where hot ash rises by buoyancy
The umbrella region, where the column spreads at its top
The caldera region, where the summit collapses inward
The gas thrust region, where gas blasts out of the vent
rationales: The convective region is where the column rises; spreading happens above it.
Correct. The umbrella region is the upper part of the column, where it spreads out sideways.
A caldera is a collapse feature on the ground, not a region of the column.
The gas thrust region is the lowest kilometre or two, right above the vent.
questions.takeaway: The flat, spreading top of a Plinian column is the umbrella region.

questions.stem: Eruption X ejects far more material, with a much taller eruption column, than eruption Y. How do they compare on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI)?
options: X has the higher VEI, as VEI reflects erupted volume and column height
Y has the higher VEI, as smaller eruptions last longer and do more harm
VEI cannot be assigned until the death tolls are known
They share a VEI if they come from the same type of volcano
rationales: Correct. VEI classifies eruptions mainly by the volume of material erupted and the height of the eruption column.
VEI is not based on duration or harm.
VEI measures the eruption, not its human impact.
VEI is based on each eruption's own size, not on the volcano type.
questions.takeaway: VEI ranks eruptions by erupted volume and column height.

questions.stem: Which set of features describes a Hawaiian-type eruption?
options: Rhyolitic, low silica, low viscosity, explosive yet still gentle
Rhyolitic, high silica, high viscosity, explosive and pumice-rich
Basaltic, high silica, high viscosity, effusive and full of ash
Basaltic, low silica, low viscosity, effusive and relatively gentle
rationales: Rhyolitic magma is high in silica, and gentle eruptions are effusive, not explosive.
These are the features of Plinian eruptions.
Basaltic magma is low in silica and low in viscosity.
Correct. Hawaiian-type eruptions are relatively gentle, low-energy and effusive, with typically basaltic, low-silica, low-viscosity (mafic) magma.
questions.takeaway: Hawaiian-type: basaltic, mafic, low viscosity, effusive.

questions.stem: What characterises the ultra-Plinian eruptions that form calderas?
options: Rhyolitic magma, small volumes and mostly effusive lava flows
Basaltic magma, small volumes and gentle, long-lived lava fountains
Rhyolitic magma, huge ejected volumes and very high energy release
Basaltic magma, huge volumes but almost no gas or ash released at all
rationales: Rhyolitic is right, but caldera eruptions are explosive and very large.
This describes gentle Hawaiian-type activity, not caldera formation.
Correct. Caldera-forming ultra-Plinian eruptions involve rhyolitic magma, very large ejecta volumes, high energy release and massive plumes.
Caldera eruptions are rhyolitic and gas-rich, producing massive plumes.
questions.takeaway: Calderas come from ultra-Plinian eruptions: rhyolitic, huge volume, high energy.

questions.stem: A steep-sided stratovolcano erupts fast-moving, fluid lava flows instead of explosions. What does this suggest?
options: Shape fixes eruption style, so the observation must be mistaken
The magma must have been high in silica, as all stratovolcanoes require
This eruption's magma was low in silica, despite the volcano's shape
The magma was cooler than usual, which made it far more fluid
rationales: Volcano shape reflects the usual magma, but each eruption's style depends on the magma erupted.
High-silica magma would be stiff and tend to erupt explosively, not as fluid flows.
Correct. Eruption style follows the magma. A stratovolcano can still erupt low-silica magma that produces fluid lava flows.
Cooler lava is stiffer, not more fluid.
questions.takeaway: Eruption style is set by the magma's silica content, which can differ from what the volcano's shape suggests.

questions.stem: Why are lava flows considered the least hazardous process in a volcanic eruption?
options: They only occur at stratovolcanoes, which are far away from where people live
They cool almost instantly in air, so they never travel beyond the vent itself
They give off no heat or gas, so they are dangerous only to the landscape
They usually move slowly enough to escape, so their main threat is to property
rationales: Lava flows are typical of shield volcanoes with fluid lava, and they can occur at stratovolcanoes too.
Lava flows can travel far, depending on temperature, silica, extrusion rate and slope.
Lava is extremely hot. It is less deadly because people can usually move out of its way.
Correct. Lava flows are the least hazardous volcanic process; their biggest hazard is to property rather than lives.
questions.takeaway: Lava flows mainly threaten property, not lives.

questions.stem: Which lava flow is likely to travel the furthest?
options: Hot, low-silica lava erupting at a high rate down a steep slope
Cool, high-silica lava erupting at a high rate down a steep slope
Hot, low-silica lava erupting at a low rate across flat ground
Cool, high-silica lava erupting at a low rate across flat ground
rationales: Correct. Flow rate and distance depend on temperature, silica content, extrusion rate and slope. Every factor here favours a long flow.
Cold or high-silica lava is viscous and will not travel far, even on a steep slope.
The lava is fluid, but a low extrusion rate and flat ground both limit how far it goes.
Every factor here limits the flow.
questions.takeaway: Lava travels furthest when it is hot, low in silica, erupted rapidly and on a steep slope.

questions.stem: What is a volcanic bomb?
options: A pocket of gas that explodes underground before an eruption has begun
Molten rock thrown out of a vent that solidifies in the air
A dense cloud of hot ash and steam that hugs the ground as it moves
A block of cold rock that rolls downslope from a collapsing lava dome
rationales: Bombs are pieces of ejected rock, not underground gas explosions.
Correct. Volcanic (lava) bombs are molten rock ejected from a volcano that solidify as they travel through the air.
That describes a pyroclastic flow.
Bombs are thrown out molten, not rolled down cold.
questions.takeaway: Volcanic bombs are molten rock ejected into the air that solidify in flight.

questions.stem: Where does pyroclastic fall come from, and how is it spread?
options: It pours from the vent as a dense flow and collects mainly in valley floors
It seeps from hot ground near the vent and collects in acid crater lakes
It rises from the gas thrust region and lands only around the crater rim
It falls from the convective part of the column and spreads widely downwind
rationales: Dense flows that collect in valleys are pyroclastic flows, not falls.
Acid lakes form from dissolved gases, not from ash fall.
Ash fall is widespread, not limited to the crater rim.
Correct. Ash (tephra) falls from the convective part of the Plinian column and can cover wide areas, travelling downwind.
questions.takeaway: Ash fall drops from the convective column and spreads widely downwind.

questions.stem: A geologist finds a volcanic ash layer of fairly even thickness draping hilltops and valley floors alike. What most likely deposited it?
options: Pyroclastic fall, which blankets the ground in a near-uniform layer
A lava flow, which follows the lowest ground away from the vent
A pyroclastic flow, which races downslope and pools in valley floors
A lahar, which carries water and rock fragments along river valleys
rationales: Correct. Fallout from the Plinian column blankets the ground with a nearly uniform mantle of fine particles, over hills and valleys alike.
Lava follows low ground and solidifies as rock, not as an even ash layer.
Pyroclastic flow deposits concentrate in valleys rather than draping hilltops.
Lahars follow valleys and would not leave an even layer on hilltops.
questions.takeaway: Fall deposits drape the landscape evenly; flow deposits fill valleys.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an impact of ash fall listed in the notes?
options: Damaging engines and reducing visibility
Triggering slip on nearby tectonic faults
Collapsing roofs under the weight of ash
Clogging water supplies and damaging crops
rationales: Ash damages engines and reduces visibility, blocking sunlight.
Correct. Ash fall is dense and disruptive, but triggering fault slip is not one of its listed impacts.
Ash is dense and can collapse roofs.
Ash clogs water supplies and damages crops.
questions.takeaway: Ash fall collapses roofs, disrupts power and water, harms breathing and crops, and damages engines.

questions.stem: Why is volcanic ash a serious hazard even to aircraft flying far from the volcano?
options: Ash reflects radar, so pilots lose track of where the ground is
Ash clouds carry lava bombs that can strike distant aircraft
Ash drifts widely downwind and can cause jet engines to fail
Ash stays near the vent but heats the air along flight paths
rationales: The notes list engine damage, abraded windows and contaminated systems, not radar effects.
Bombs fall close to the vent; distant aircraft face fine ash.
Correct. Ash plumes drift over large areas, and ash damages jet engines, abrades windows and contaminates aircraft systems. Engine failure is the major issue.
Ash travels far downwind; the danger is ash entering the engines, not heated air.
questions.takeaway: Ash drifts far and can cause jet engine failure, so aircraft avoid it.

questions.stem: An airline argues it can safely fly through a thin volcanic ash cloud because the concentration is low. What does the aviation guidance in the notes say?
options: Fly through only if the ash is below a safe threshold
Fly higher, because ash never reaches cruising height
Avoid volcanic ash, regardless of its concentration
Fly through quickly to limit time spent in the ash
rationales: The guidance sets no safe concentration; it says to avoid ash whatever the concentration.
Plinian columns can reach the stratosphere, well above cruising height.
Correct. The recommended procedure for volcanic ash, regardless of concentration, is to avoid it.
Even brief exposure can cause engine failure, so the guidance is to avoid ash.
questions.takeaway: Aviation rule for volcanic ash: avoid it, whatever the concentration.

questions.stem: A large eruption grounds flights across a continent for a week. Which impact reaches furthest from the volcano?
options: Lost perishable goods and halted factories far from the eruption
Lava flows destroying houses that stand on the volcano's lower flanks
Roofs collapsing under heavy ash fall in towns right beside the volcano
Lahars flowing down the river valleys that drain the volcano's slopes
rationales: Correct. Cancelled flights disrupt travel, cause perishable goods to be lost and suspend industrial production far from the volcano, with large economic costs.
Lava flows are local to the volcano's flanks.
Roof collapse is a local impact near the volcano.
Lahars affect valleys draining the volcano, not distant economies.
questions.takeaway: Airspace closures spread an eruption's economic impact far beyond the volcano.

questions.stem: After a very large explosive eruption, global temperatures drop for a short time. What causes this?
options: Carbon dioxide from the eruption traps heat close to the ground
Sulphur dioxide forms sulphate aerosols that reflect sunlight
Ash fall blankets the oceans and stops them giving off heat
Lava flows draw heat out of the atmosphere as they slowly cool
rationales: Trapping heat would warm the surface, not cool it.
Correct. SO₂ spreads globally and forms sulphate aerosols that reflect sunlight, temporarily cooling Earth's climate.
The global effect comes from aerosols in the atmosphere, not ash on the ocean.
Lava flows are far too local to change global temperature.
questions.takeaway: Volcanic SO₂ forms sulphate aerosols that reflect sunlight and briefly cool the climate.

questions.stem: Animals are found dead in a low hollow on a volcano's flank, though there has been no eruption. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A pyroclastic surge swept unseen over the ridge and down into the hollow
Acid rain from the crater lake poisoned the water that they drank there
Volcanic SO₂ formed aerosols that blocked out sunlight inside the hollow
Dense volcanic CO₂ pooled near the ground and suffocated them
rationales: A surge happens during an eruption, and there has been none.
Acid crater lakes are a real hazard, but suffocation in a low hollow points to heavy CO₂.
Aerosols affect sunlight on a regional or global scale, not suffocation in a hollow.
Correct. Volcanoes often leak gas. CO₂ is denser than air, so it sits near the ground, and animals, including people, can suffocate in this odourless gas.
questions.takeaway: Volcanic CO₂ is denser than air, pools in low areas and can suffocate.

questions.stem: Trees on part of a volcano's flank die off, though no eruption has occurred. The soil gas contains very high levels of CO₂. How does this kill them?
options: The CO₂ makes the soil acidic enough to dissolve the roots directly
The CO₂ heats the soil until the roots are cooked where they grow
Roots are denied oxygen, and their uptake of nutrients is disrupted
The leaves take in too much CO₂ and so stop producing any oxygen
rationales: The mechanism given is oxygen starvation of the roots, not acid dissolving them.
The gas is not killing trees through heat.
Correct. Leaves make oxygen from CO₂, but roots need to absorb oxygen directly. High soil CO₂ denies roots oxygen and interferes with nutrient uptake.
The problem is in the soil around the roots, not in the leaves.
questions.takeaway: High CO₂ in soil kills plants by starving their roots of oxygen.

questions.stem: A crater lake suddenly releases a huge volume of gas, which flows downhill as a dense, fast cloud. What is this?
options: A sector collapse, as the lake's weight breaks the volcano's flank
A limnic eruption, releasing CO₂ that was dissolved in the lake
A lahar, made of water and rock rushing out of the crater lake
A pyroclastic flow, made of hot ash and steam from the crater
rationales: A sector collapse is a landslide of the volcano's flank, not a gas release.
Correct. A limnic eruption is a sudden release of CO₂ from a lake, creating a dense, fast flow of gas.
A lahar is a mixture of water and rock, not a cloud of gas.
A pyroclastic flow is hot ash and steam from an eruption, not gas from a lake.
questions.takeaway: Limnic eruption: sudden CO₂ release from a lake, flowing downhill as dense gas.

questions.stem: Why can volcanic crater lakes become extremely acidic?
options: Gases from the magma, such as SO₂ and CO₂, dissolve in the water
Lava flows heat the water until it breaks down into strong acid
Ash from the column adds silica that turns the lake water acidic
Rain is naturally acidic and evaporates to concentrate the lake
rationales: Correct. Crater lakes become strongly acidic as gases from magma, such as CO₂, SO₂ and HCl, dissolve in the water.
Heating water does not turn it into acid.
Silica from ash is not what makes crater lakes acidic.
The acidity comes from magmatic gases, not from concentrated rain.
questions.takeaway: Acid crater lakes form when magmatic gases dissolve in the water.

questions.stem: Which description fits a pyroclastic flow?
options: A mixture of water and loose rock fragments flowing down steep slopes
A dilute, turbulent cloud rich in gas that can rise over hills and ridges
Fine ash falling from the eruption column and blanketing land downwind
A dense, hot mixture of ash and steam that hugs the ground as it flows
rationales: That describes a lahar.
That describes a pyroclastic surge, which has a higher ratio of gas to rock.
That describes pyroclastic fall.
Correct. A pyroclastic flow is a dense mixture of hot volcanic ash and steam flowing downslope and hugging the ground.
questions.takeaway: Pyroclastic flow: dense, hot, ground-hugging ash and steam.

questions.stem: One hot volcanic cloud crosses a ridge and reaches the next valley, while another stays confined to the valley floor where it started. What best distinguishes them?
options: The first is ash fall carried along by the wind, while the second is a lava flow
The first is a surge, whose extra gas makes it turbulent enough to cross ridges
The first is a lahar, which is fluid enough to overtop any obstacle in its path
The first is a flow, whose greater density gives it the momentum to carry over ridges
rationales: Both clouds are moving across the ground, which fits pyroclastic density currents rather than ash fall and lava.
Correct. A pyroclastic surge has a higher ratio of gas to rock, making it more turbulent and able to rise over ridges and hills. A dense pyroclastic flow concentrates in valleys.
A lahar is water and rock and follows valleys; it is not a hot cloud.
Density keeps a pyroclastic flow low and in valleys; it is the dilute surge that crosses ridges.
questions.takeaway: Surges (more gas) cross ridges; flows (denser) stay in valleys.

questions.stem: Compared with a pyroclastic flow, a pyroclastic surge has:
options: A lower ratio of gas to rock, making it denser and slower
No ash at all, being made of nothing but steam and gas
A higher ratio of gas to rock, making it more turbulent
Water in place of gas, making it a kind of volcanic mudflow
rationales: This describes how a flow differs from a surge, not the other way round.
Surges still carry ash and rock; they simply have more gas relative to rock.
Correct. The surge's higher gas-to-rock ratio makes it more turbulent and able to rise over ridges.
A volcanic mudflow is a lahar, not a surge.
questions.takeaway: Surge vs flow: more gas, more turbulence.

questions.stem: Which statement about lahars is correct?
options: They are clouds of hot ash and steam that form only in explosive eruptions
They are slow lava flows that occur only at shield volcanoes with fluid magma
They are gas releases from crater lakes that suffocate animals downslope
They are water and rock mixtures that rain can trigger long after eruptions
rationales: Hot ash-and-steam clouds are pyroclastic flows.
Lahars are not lava.
Gas releases from lakes are limnic eruptions.
Correct. Lahars are mixtures of water and loose rock fragments flowing down steep volcano slopes. They can be triggered by an eruption or by heavy rain, so they are an ongoing hazard.
questions.takeaway: Lahars: water plus loose rock, triggered by eruptions or rain, an ongoing hazard.

questions.stem: Years after an eruption has ended, a town on a river downstream of the volcano is still judged to be at risk. From which hazard, chiefly?
options: Lahars, since heavy rain can mobilise loose volcanic debris on the slopes
Ash fall, which keeps settling out of the original eruption for years
Pyroclastic surges, which can sweep down long after an eruption is over
Lava bombs, which can keep falling for years after an eruption has ended
rationales: Correct. Loose volcanic debris remains on the slopes, and heavy rain can turn it into lahars that race down river valleys.
Ash settles within days to weeks; the long-term threat downstream is lahars.
Surges happen during eruptions, not years afterwards.
Bombs are thrown out during an eruption only.
questions.takeaway: Lahars keep volcanoes dangerous long after eruptions end.

questions.stem: A growing city is built on top of an old lahar deposit in a valley below a volcano. What does that deposit tell planners?
options: The ground is now safe, since old deposits block any new flows
Only ash fall threatens the city, as lahars never repeat a path
The volcano is extinct, since lahars only follow a final eruption
Lahars have reached this ground before and could reach it again
rationales: Old deposits do not protect against new lahars; they mark where lahars go.
Lahars follow valleys, so they tend to reuse the same paths.
Lahars can be triggered by eruptions or heavy rain; a deposit says nothing about the volcano being extinct.
Correct. An old lahar deposit shows the valley is a lahar pathway, and many communities built on such deposits are at risk.
questions.takeaway: Old lahar deposits mark the paths future lahars are likely to take.

questions.stem: A large section of an ocean island volcano's flank suddenly collapses into the sea. Which follow-on hazard is most likely?
options: A lahar, as the collapse empties the crater lake down the far slope
Acid rain, as the collapse mixes seawater with the crater lake gases
A tsunami, as the collapse suddenly displaces a huge volume of water
A limnic eruption, as the collapse releases CO₂ held in the seafloor
rationales: A collapse into the sea mainly displaces seawater; nothing suggests a crater lake is involved.
This is not a mechanism described in the notes.
Correct. Sector collapses on volcanic islands can generate tsunamis, which can travel across ocean basins.
Limnic eruptions come from gas-charged lakes, not from flank collapse.
questions.takeaway: Volcanic flank collapse into the sea can generate a tsunami.

questions.stem: Beneath a volcano, seismometers record sharp earthquakes like those on tectonic faults, together with long-lasting tremor. What do these signals suggest?
options: Brittle rock failure, plus resonance from moving magma and gas
Old magma cooling and cracking as it contracts into solid rock
Only tectonic faulting, unrelated to any magma below the volcano
That an eruption has already begun at the surface of the volcano
rationales: Correct. Volcanic seismicity includes brittle failure of rock, like on a tectonic fault, and a variety of signals from resonance due to magma and gas movement.
The notes link these signals to brittle failure and moving magma and gas, not cooling.
The tremor points to magma and gas moving, not just tectonic faulting.
These signals track movement within the volcano and can come before an eruption.
questions.takeaway: Volcano seismicity = brittle rock failure + resonance from moving magma and gas.

questions.stem: Seismic tomography beneath a volcano reveals a zone where seismic waves travel unusually slowly. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Cold, solid rock, which slows waves more than hot rock does
Hot, partially molten rock, a possible zone of stored magma
An empty cavity left behind when the last eruption drained
A layer of loose, water-soaked ash lying at the surface
rationales: This reverses the relationship: cooler, solid rock is faster.
Correct. Seismic waves travel more slowly through hot, partially molten rock than through cooler solid rock, so slow zones mark possible magma.
Tomography is used to find magma storage, and slow zones point to hot, partly molten rock.
Tomography images the volcano's interior, not surface ash.
questions.takeaway: Slow seismic-wave zones beneath a volcano point to hot, partially molten rock.

questions.stem: Why is infrasound well suited to monitoring volcanoes in remote regions?
options: It measures magma temperature directly, without anyone visiting the volcano
Low-frequency sound from explosions travels far, reaching distant stations
It samples gas from the air, identifying volcanic emissions from far away
It needs a dense network on the volcano's flanks, which remote areas have
rationales: Infrasound records sound waves, not temperature.
Correct. Infrasound is very low-frequency sound from explosions and gas and magma movement. It can be recorded by stations far from the volcano.
Gas monitoring is a separate method; infrasound records sound.
Remote volcanoes lack dense networks; that is why infrasound is needed.
questions.takeaway: Infrasound is the method for monitoring distant volcanoes.

questions.stem: Thermal imaging shows strong hydrothermal activity at a volcano. What can be concluded from this alone?
options: The volcano is extinct, as only leftover heat remains
Magma is rising quickly, so an eruption must be imminent
Magma is present at depth, but it is not necessarily moving
Groundwater has cooled the magma so it can no longer erupt
rationales: Hydrothermal activity shows that magma is present, which an extinct volcano would lack.
Heat alone does not show movement; other signals such as deformation or seismicity are needed.
Correct. Hydrothermal activity demonstrates the presence of magma, not necessarily magma movement.
Hydrothermal activity does not show the magma has been made harmless.
questions.takeaway: Hydrothermal activity shows magma is present, not that it is moving.

questions.stem: GPS stations around a volcano show the ground slowly rising and moving outward over several years. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Deflation, as magma drains away from the chamber underneath
